title: Oracle files to sell $20 billion in new stock, bonds to finance AI buildout
summary: Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue stock new shares and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout.
body: Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue new stock and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout. The hyperscaler will sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. While the fundraising was already outlined at an investor day last week , shares tumbled more than 6% Monday. "This seems to be exactly what they previewed," said Rob Oliver, senior research analyst at Baird. "So I'm not sure why the market is freaking about it." Oracle said it plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, repayments of debt and future investments. The hyperscaler's stock initially bounced after last Wednesday's investor day, when Oracle also issued a revenue forecast of at least $225 billion for fiscal 2030. At the time Oracle also said it was limiting its additional capital market funding for the fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to that $20 billion. "This is a major relief given concerns about the state of debt markets and the cost of capital (although UBS has argued that these debt market concerns have been over-stated)," UBS analyst Karl Keirstead said in a note on Thursday. Oracle plans to turn to vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments to help it transition to positive free cash flow, which it expects to reach in the second half of 2028. Stock and bonds in Oracle, co-founded by former CEO Larry Ellison, have been under pressure amid growing investor concerns about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure. Oracle shares are down 33% in 2026 and 50% over the past 12 months. The yield on its investment-grade 4.95% bond due in 2031 is currently 7.267%. The sentiment shift is also seen in Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default. The spread sits at 296, up 270% in one year. That's more in line with a high-end junk bond rating, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence's Gavan Nolan. While still an investment-grade credit, Oracle was downgraded by S&P to a BBB- in July, one rating level above high yield. It has $125.34 billion in debt, as of Aug. 31, with the bulk in senior notes. What ultimately matters for Oracle is execution, Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners, said in an email to CNBC Monday. "Can they do what they say they are going to do? We view this as the narrative across the AI space," he said. "If this gets executed according to plans laid out, they will be rewarded. If they have to come back to market in the back half of '27 after telling everyone this was the last of the capital needed ... look out."

Chief sustainability officer Aurélien Hamelle told reporters that demand could fall faster if EV sales keep growing. In November 2025, TotalEnergies forecast oil demand rising nearly 5% to 108 million barrels per day by 2040 under current trends, before easing to 98 million bpd by 2050. It cited the partial rollback of U.S. green subsidies, new LNG approvals, new coal plants in Asia and slower EV sales. CEO Patrick Pouyanné said at the time that the chances of the Paris-aligned scenario were “diminishing, even out of reach.” A year earlier, the company had expected demand to peak after 2030 . The 2026 report says the energy crisis set off by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran could act as an “accelerator” of the transition. It points to a sharp rise in EV sales in Asia, Latin America and Europe, and to higher biofuel blending mandates. Hamelle described a “stunning acceleration” of low-carbon technology between the second quarter of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026. The International Energy Agency (IEA) projects about 23 million EV sales in 2026, close to 30% of new cars worldwide. In the first quarter, EV sales rose roughly 30% in Europe, 80% in Asia-Pacific outside China and 75% in Latin America. Gasoline-only cars fell below half of global new car sales for the first time in the first half of the year, at 49%. body: Oil Prices Plunge 7% as U.S. and Iran Signal Room for Diplomacy Oil prices plunged nearly 7% on Monday after Washington and Tehran both signaled they would give diplomacy a chance, wiping out part of the war premium that lifted crude through October. Brent traded at $105.60 per barrel, down $7.85, and WTI fell $7.20 to $96.92. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Monday that the Supreme Leader has granted the government “certain authorities” over peace talks and that Tehran “will try to resolve the problem with dialogue,” state media reported . Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said negotiators in Qatar are working on a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz in as little as two days if Washington meets a series of conditions. He said Tehran, which has demanded an end to the U.S. naval blockade of its ports, the lifting of oil sanctions and a halt to fighting on all regional fronts, is not holding direct talks with the United States. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that no decision had been made on new strikes and that President Trump prefers a diplomatic resolution. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu urged Trump in a Saturday call to resume strikes immediately after Tuesday’s midterm elections, and Trump said he wants to give the talks more time. Asked whether he would return to war this week, Trump said: “Let’s say I did. Would I tell you?” Traders had been bracing for a new escalation after the vote, and Brent briefly reached $118 in October. Goldman Sachs estimates that a geopolitical risk premium of about $27 per barrel accounts for most of that rally. The bank raised its December Brent forecast to $105 from $90 and expects Brent to average $88 in 2027, up from $80. ANZ sees Brent ending 2026 at $105, and UBS at $110. Goldman’s Daan Struyven said the premium would come off quickly only with “a diplomatic solution that market participants see as sustainable.” The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre reported a projectile hitting a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday , days after a tanker fire in the strait pushed Brent to $117. title: St Barbara to restart Touquoy amid federal review hurdle
summary: Gold operations in Nova Scotia, Canada, are set to resume this week, but a new environmental assessment clouds the miner's expansion plans.
body: St Barbara (ASX:SBM) is set to restart ore processing at its Touquoy gold mine in Nova Scotia on Tuesday, Nov. 3, following provincial regulatory approval, even as a new federal assessment requirement raises uncertainty over its nearby 15-Mile Processing Hub Project. The Australian gold miner has completed mill refurbishments and expects commissioning and operations to ramp up through November and December. The site, about 70 km northeast of Halifax, has been inactive since mining stopped in 2023 after the company failed to secure approvals to extend operations beyond its original mine plan. “The revised mine plans for the 15-Mile Processing Hub Project reflect years of work to redesign and incorporate feedback from First Nations and neighbouring communities to achieve an exceptional design for the collective projects to achieve dramatically improved impacts,” St Barbara managing director and CEO Andrew Strelein said in a statement. The restart provides St Barbara with a path towards renewed production in Nova Scotia, where the provincial government has been encouraging mineral development. An additional federal review, however, could complicate the company’s longer-term strategy to establish a regional processing hub, with construction targeted for mid-2028. The Impact Assessment Agency of Canada has imposed a federal assessment requirement on the 15-Mile project , although St Barbara said federal officials expect the process to conclude before construction is scheduled to begin. The company plans to engage with federal and provincial authorities over the next three weeks to determine whether the decision will increase costs, create administrative complexity or threaten its development timetable. St Barbara has also begun contingency planning to resume open-pit mining at Touquoy should the assessment delay its processing hub plans. The miner supports Canada’s proposed Bill C-39 , which it says would establish reasonable timelines for federal permit applications. The latest developments follow provincial approval granted in April to St Barbara subsidiary Atlantic Mining Nova Scotia to reprocess about three million tonnes of ore at Touquoy. Premier Tim Houston’s government has sought to expand mineral exploration and development across the province, with mining claims and licences rising sharply over the past year. The federal assessment adds a potential obstacle to those ambitions, highlighting the challenges mining companies face when navigating overlapping provincial and federal approval processes. St Barbara has defined an initial underground mineral resource estimate at its Old Austen Mine Down-Plunge prospect, also in Nova Scotia, adding another potential source of gold to its regional development plans. The resource contains an estimated 500,000 ouncesof gold in 4.8 million tonnes grading an average 3.4 grams per tonne. The estimate incorporates mineable stope optimization constraints to define underground resource geometry beyond the previously reported mineral resource for the Old Austen open pit. St Barbara is planning an extensive drilling program to further test the deposit and improve confidence in its underground resource estimates. The results could help determine the scale of future underground mining opportunities as the company works to restore operations at Touquoy and advance its processing hub through the permitting process. The stock rose. Hudbay is to invest C$30.1 million, while the unnamed investor committed C$19.7 million, Pecoy said Monday . Each would hold just under 10% after closing, calculated on a partially diluted basis. “We view the deal positively, as it validates Pecoy’s technical and geological quality, while strengthening the balance sheet at lower dilution than we had modelled,” Desjardins Capital Markets mining analyst Bryce Adams wrote Monday in a note. The investment connects Pecoy with a producer that operates the Constancia copper mine in Peru. It also provides funding for drilling and studies needed to better define the deposit and assess how its metals could be recovered. Given Hudbay’s long history of operating in southern Peru, “we view their investment as providing a strong endorsement to the future potential of the Pecoy project,” National Bank Financial mining analyst Andrew Dusome said in a separate note. Pecoy shares jumped 5.5% to C$1.92 Monday morning in Toronto, valuing the company at about C$405 million ($289 million). The stock has traded between C85¢ and C$2.29 in the past year. Vancouver-based Pecoy plans to issue about 24.7 million shares at C$2.02 apiece, a 10% premium to its 10-day volume-weighted average price through Oct. 30. The subscription price is also 11% above Friday’s C$1.82 close. Closing is expected around Thursday, subject to regulatory approvals, including TSX Venture Exchange acceptance. Hudbay would receive rights to participate in future financings and top up its holdings to maintain ownership of up to 9.9%. Subject to ownership thresholds, it could nominate one director, or two if Pecoy’s board expands to at least 10 members. Both Hudbay and the unnamed investor had previously invested in Pecoy, CEO Vincent Metcalfe told The Northern Miner Monday via e-mail. Hudbay built its position through market acquisitions, while the second investor holds historical warrants, which haven’t been exercised yet, Metcalfe said. The latest financing would lift Pecoy’s cash resources to roughly C$70 million, enough for five to six quarters of spending, Adams said. His model had assumed a C$50-million financing at C$1.50 a share, requiring about 33.3 million new shares. The financing “also improves funding visibility through the next phase of resource definition and technical work,” Scotiabank mining analyst Eric Winmill wrote Monday. The explorer owns the Pecoy and Tororume projects in southern Peru’s Arequipa region. Pecoy lies about 275 km northwest of Arequipa, at an elevation of about 1,650 metres, near highway, power and port infrastructure. An April 2025 resource estimate outlined 865 million inferred tonnes grading 0.34% copper, 0.012% molybdenum, 0.05 gram gold per tonne and 1.33 grams silver for contained metal of about 6.45 billion lb. copper. The estimate uses a 0.23% copper cut-off. These resources have not demonstrated economic viability. Tororume, 8 km to the north, provides another exploration target. Previous owner Pembrook completed nine widely spaced drill holes between 2017 and 2023, intersecting copper and molybdenum mineralization. Pecoy says much of the system remains untested. The new money will support resource expansion, geological work and metallurgical testing ahead of an updated Pecoy resource estimate. Adams expects that estimate early next year and a preliminary economic assessment later in 2027. title: Endeavour halts Burkina gold underground as ramp sinks
summary: The Oct. 28 incident is another setback for an operation set to miss its annual production target.
body: Endeavour Mining (TSX, LSE: EDV) suspended underground mining at its Mana gold mine in Burkina Faso after part of an access road sank, adding another setback at an operation already expected to miss its annual production target. The Oct. 28 incident restricted access to two underground entrances, Dangouna and Aviera, through the depleted Wona open pit, Endeavour said Monday. Workers were evacuated, nobody was injured and local authorities were notified. Mining has been stopped at all three active underground entrances while specialists assess ground stability and repairs. Endeavour didn’t immediately disclose the cause of the incident or announce a restart date. Despite the incident, Endeavour said it remains on track to hit full-year production and all-in sustaining cost targets even if no further mining occurs at Mana in the fourth quarter. Endeavour previously said it expected 2026 output to range between 1.09 million oz. and 1.27 million ounces. “The overall impact will depend on how long portal remediation takes (we think one to two quarters) and on whether open pit feed, subject to permitting, can supplement throughput,” National Bank Financial mining analyst Mohamed Sidibé said Monday in a note. Endeavour is considering restarting and accelerating mining through the Wona entrance, which remains accessible, and drawing on nearby open pits to limit lost production. It plans to outline the ground assessment and repair plan when it reports third-quarter results on Nov. 12. The disruption follows an earlier ground-stability concern. In July, Endeavour disclosed that mining at Aviera had paused that month to monitor a surface fracture in the depleted Wona pit above the deposit. At the time, it said the fracture didn’t affect active ore zones and anticipated resuming work around mid-third quarter, subject to monitoring. Monday’s announcement didn’t say whether that fracture and the latest subsidence were connected. The event disclosed Monday “appears to have occurred on a structure parallel to the July one, though it is too early to tell if they are related,” Sidibé said. Mana represents about 5% of the company’s net asset value, according to his calculations. Along with the Houndé mine, Mana is one of Endeavour’s two producing assets in Burkina Faso. In West Africa, the company also produces gold in Côte d’Ivoire and Senegal. Mana’s difficulties also extend beyond ground conditions. Endeavour warned in July that annual output would fall below the bottom of its original 155,000–180,000 oz. target, with sustaining costs exceeding guidance. It attributed the weakness partly to earlier depletion of the higher-grade Siou underground deposit after unsuccessful drilling to extend its resources, and delayed mining at the Bana Camp open pit. First-half production fell to 68,000 oz. from 87,000 oz. a year earlier, a decline of about 22%. Mana accounted for about 12% of Endeavour’s first-half output. London-based Endeavour owns 85% of Mana, with Burkina Faso’s government holding the balance. The mine lies about 60 km north of Houndé. Mana’s processing plant began operating in 2008, and the mine shifted to fully underground production in 2024. It produced 173,000 oz. last year. Endeavour’s longer-term strategy is to extend its operating life beyond a decade by expanding underground deposits and evaluating nearby surface targets. Restoring reliable access to those underground workings is now the immediate priority for the operation.Top of FormBottom of Form Toronto-traded shares of Endeavour rose 0.9% to C$70.33 Monday morning, valuing the company at about C$17 billion ($12.2 billion). title: Ontario fast-tracks Mayfair’s Fenn-Gib gold project
summary: The Fenn-Gib gold project is the fourth chosen under the province's One Project, One Process framework.
body: Ontario has added Mayfair Gold’s (TSXV: MFG; NYSE-A: MINE) Fenn-Gib gold project to its accelerated permitting program, making the proposed development near Timmins the fourth selected under the province’s One Project, One Process framework. The designation puts provincial approvals and Indigenous consultation under a coordinated review led by the Ministry of Energy and Mines. Mayfair is targeting a construction start in 2028 and first production in 2030, while Ontario estimates the project would support 450 construction jobs and 250 long-term positions. “For too long, permitting delays stood in the way of getting Ontario’s resources to market,” Energy and Mines Minister Stephen Lecce said in a statement Monday. “To compete, we must be the best, which is why our government is planning to further accelerate permitting this fall, to get mines built faster, unlocking billions in investment to create more good-paying jobs right here at home.” The decision advances Mayfair’s effort to develop a smaller, higher-grade starter operation within Fenn-Gib’s much larger gold resource. The proposed package comprises a C$300-million project loan and a C$10-million equity investment, compared with Fenn-Gib’s estimated C$450-million initial development cost. Macquarie completed the investment on Oct. 14, buying about 2.35 million shares at C$4.26 apiece. The proposed debt financing remains subject to due diligence, definitive agreements and closing conditions, Mayfair said. The loan proposal includes an early C$25-million drawdown to support work ahead of full construction financing, including engineering, equipment orders and preliminary construction activities. The proposed debt would cover about two-thirds of initial capital costs, leaving Mayfair to arrange the balance. January’s prefeasibility study focused on probable reserves of 25.1 million tonnes grading 1.29 grams gold per tonne for about 1 million oz. contained metal. title: Gold Fields clears major hurdle for Quebec’s Windfall gold mine
summary: Quebec grants environmental approval for Windfall, advancing a high-grade project toward a 2027 investment decision.
body: Gold Fields (NYSE, JSE: GFI) has received a key environmental authorization for its high-grade Windfall gold project in Quebec, clearing a major regulatory hurdle as the company prepares for a final investment decision. The certificate, issued by Quebec’s Ministry of the Environment, confirms the project has completed its environmental and social impact assessment under the province’s Environment Quality Act. It allows construction to proceed subject to regulatory conditions, although Gold Fields must still secure a mining lease and secondary permits. “Receiving the Certificate of Authorization for Windfall is a major milestone for Gold Fields and for one of Canada’s highest-grade development-stage gold projects,” CEO Mike Fraser said in the statement. The approval brings Gold Fields closer to developing a mine expected to produce about 300,000 oz. of gold annually once fully ramped up. The company is targeting a final investment decision by February 2027, positioning Windfall as a potential long-life, low-cost operation in Quebec’s Eeyou Istchee James Bay region. The authorization follows a setback in late September , when Gold Fields suspended underground development at Windfall after an exploration-work permit expired. The proposed $1.9-billion mine had also been awaiting separate provincial environmental approval. The authorization follows the June 2026 signing of the Uukiimau Agreement with the Cree First Nation of Waswanipi, the Cree Nation Government and the Grand Council of the Crees. The impact and benefit agreement establishes a framework for Indigenous participation and economic benefits from the development. The environmental review involved several years of technical studies, community consultations and government assessments. Quebec’s Environmental and Social Impact Review Committee (COMEX) examined the project, including through public hearings in Lebel-sur-Quévillon and Waswanipi in spring 2026. “The Uukiimau Agreement and the Certificate of Authorization demonstrate how responsible mining can be advanced through respect, transparency and shared value creation,” Fraser said. Windfall lies on the traditional territory of the Cree First Nation of Waswanipi, about 115 km by road east of Lebel-sur-Quévillon. Windfall Mining Group, a wholly owned Gold Fields subsidiary, is developing the deposit. Gold Fields acquired full ownership of Windfall in October 2024 through its C$2.16-billion takeover of Osisko Mining , following a C$300-million investment for an initial 50% stake in May 2023. The project could generate employment, business opportunities for Indigenous and local companies, and broader economic benefits for the region. Its development will also test Gold Fields’ ability to translate regulatory approvals and community commitments into a commercially viable mining operation. Gold Fields plans to begin remobilizing personnel and equipment to Windfall shortly, with site operations, including underground activities, expected to resume progressively. The company intends to finalize its execution plan before making a construction commitment. It expects to announce its investment decision alongside its provisional 2026 financial results by February 2027. Despite the environmental approval, construction remains dependent on outstanding permits and the investment decision. Gold Fields must also complete its planning before advancing the project into full development. Beyond the main deposit, Windfall offers district-scale exploration potential. Gold Fields controls approximately 2,500 sq. km in the Urban-Barry and Quévillon areas, where regional exploration is targeting additional gold discoveries. The company sees opportunities to expand the mineral inventory along strike and at depth, potentially extending the operation’s life beyond its initial development plan. UK inflation jumps to 3.5% — cementing rate hike expectations
summary: U.K. inflation rose by a hotter-than-expected 3.5% in the 12 months to September, driven by the surging cost of motor fuels.
body: U.K. inflation rose by a hotter-than-expected 3.5% in the 12 months to September, driven by the surging cost of motor fuels. Economists polled by Reuters had been forecasting an annual inflation rate of 3.4%. September's print marked a continuation of the U.K.'s upward trend for inflation, which came in at 3.1% in August and 2.9% in July. The September reading was the highest annual inflation figure in almost a year. The U.K.'s Office for National Statistics said on Wednesday that the motor fuel inflation rate had hit its highest level since August 2022, when fuel costs surged in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Britain is a net energy importer, making it vulnerable to external energy shocks, such as the U.S.-Iran war and the subsequent struggle to move oil through the Strait of Hormuz. U.K. motor fuel prices surged 29.8% in the year to September, ONS data showed on Wednesday. The British pound was flat against both the euro and the U.S. dollar following the data release, and yields on U.K. government bonds were also little changed. Scott Gardner, investment strategist at J.P. Morgan Personal Investing, said in a note Wednesday morning that recent growth in headline inflation had "undone the progress we saw in the spring." "Bank of England policymakers will be looking beyond the headline figure," he said. "Services inflation, in particular, has accelerated in recent months which will create concern that we are starting to see second round inflationary effects beyond energy prices. While we face a different set of challenges compared to 2021, the prolonged conflict is weighing on the U.K. economy and making the case for a rate hike stronger." Markets are pricing in a 98% chance that the Bank of England raises its key interest rate by 25 basis points to 4% next month, according to LSEG data, with the majority of traders also pricing in a further hike of the same size at the central bank's final meeting of the year in December. Wednesday's expected rise in inflation also complicates the fiscal picture for the U.K. government and its finance minister. Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey is set to unveil his first fiscal shakeup next week during the U.K.'s hotly anticipated Autumn Budget. He is tasked with sticking to the previous government's so-called fiscal rules, which aim to rein in public debt while delivering on promises to soften the blow of surging consumer costs. But separate data published Wednesday showed the U.K.'s national debt was estimated to have exceeded £3 trillion ($4 trillion) in September for the first time. The cost of servicing those debts has risen drastically over the past year, and the British economy is struggling to grow . Healey said in a statement following Wednesday's data release that he would be "maintaining our fiscal discipline" in the budget next week, while working to "drive for growth [and give] businesses and families some breathing space." Suren Thiru, chief economist at the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales, said in a note Wednesday morning that rising inflation is turning the Autumn Budget into "a perilous high-wire act for the Chancellor." He said surging prices were "increasing pressure for cost-of-living support while pushing up government borrowing costs, which is shrinking fiscal headroom and narrowing his policy options." "With inflation increasing, the pieces are falling firmly into place for a November rate rise," he said. "Policymakers will also be looking to the Chancellor to avoid adding fuel to the inflation fire by delivering a credible, fiscally disciplined Budget."

title: Housing is flashing warning signs just as the Fed weighs more interest rate hikes
summary: Housing data deteriorated further in September, according to separate reports Tuesday.
body: The Federal Reserve's inflation fight is running into a growing complication: The housing market is slumping even as broader price pressures persist. Housing data deteriorated further in September , according to separate reports Tuesday, adding to an already complicated policy landscape for the central bank as it contemplates its next move on interest rates. Things appear poised to get worse before they get better. If the Fed raises short-term rates as expected over the next several months, mortgage rates that are already at 7.43% could push even higher, putting a further damper on affordability. Higher home borrowing costs have coincided with a general rise in inflation and a housing shortage. "The housing market is about to go into a deep sleep unless Washington can do a 180 on its policies and make the cost of a new home more affordable," wrote Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds. "It is not winter yet but housing is going into a deep freeze." The National Association of Realtors reported that pending sales, a forward-looking index that measures home sales under agreement but not completed, hit an all-time low in records that stretch back to 2001. The index slid 7.3% for the month and was off 11.3% from a year ago. The Wall Street estimate was for a decline of just 0.4%. Housing starts, another important metric when evaluating the state of the market, also posted a decline well outside already-muted expectations Tuesday. Privately owned housing starts fell 5.2% on the month, against expectations for a decline of just 0.4%, while building permits were off 0.2%, against the Dow Jones consensus outlook for a 2% gain, according to Commerce Department data. Moreover, single-family permits totaled just 845,000, down 4% from August and the lowest number since 2023. "Market conditions weakened in September due to fast-rising mortgage rates," said Lawrence Yun, the NAR's chief economist. "Although job growth and income gains can support home purchases, housing affordability is more affected by changes in mortgage rates." The rate for a 30-year mortgage was above 7% for most of September, ending the month around 7.6%, according to Mortgage News Daily . Five years ago, rates were closer to 3%, feeding into the Covid-era housing boom that saw an explosion in demand and, consequently, prices. Outside of the pending sales number, home builder sentiment is at lows not seen in 14 years. Under some conditions, Fed officials might respond to the housing weakness with easier monetary policy. Lower rates generally help spur demand by lowering borrowing costs. But the Fed has a bigger fight on its hands in its effort to bring inflation under control. Readings last week on consumer and producer prices provided few signs of optimism, with wholesale final demand goods prices rising 2.6%, the fastest pace in a Bureau of Labor Statistics data series going back to December 2009. Fed officials have said they are tracking the inflationary effects of the robust investment in artificial intelligence, which is driving up the cost of chips and electronics. At the same time, they believe that benefits from AI investment could offset weaker sectors of the economy such as housing. However, conditions generally point to a housing market likely to weaken further before stabilizing, Goldman Sachs economist Ronnie Walker said in a client note Monday. "In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability—reignited by the recent rebound in mortgage rates—to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity," Walker wrote. "Sustained higher mortgage rates will continue to have their most pronounced impact on housing turnover, and the recent run-up in rates is likely to push existing home sales lower in the coming months." Several data points tell the story: More than 95% of mortgage borrowers have rates below the prevailing level, and 65% are 2 percentage points below. summary: Investors expect the Fed to pause rate hikes in October, but Kevin Warsh's rejection of traditional communications practices and continued concern about inflation leave the decision uncertain.
body: Traders are betting overwhelmingly that the Federal Reserve won't raise interest rates when it meets later this month. But that judgment rests in part on assumptions about how the Fed communicates that may no longer hold under its new chairman. Kevin Warsh has left room to maneuver toward a hike, should he choose to use it. To be clear, Warsh said outright at an International Monetary Fund event in Bangkok Friday morning that he wasn't signaling a decision one way or the other. His remarks nonetheless reinforced a judgment in the markets that the Fed would pause its rate increases, with the futures market assigning a 15% probability to an October hike as of Friday morning. That judgment follows remarks by other Fed speakers, including the chair's traditional top lieutenants, who indicated they were comfortable holding. There are good reasons for investors to expect the Fed to wait. But there is also a case in the inflation data that Warsh could invoke to push the Federal Open Market Committee toward an increase on Oct. 28. Investors are overlooking that case based on longstanding past experience with the Fed. But the chairman has repeatedly rejected the convention of telling markets what he plans to do before the committee meets. That raises the possibility that investors are dangerously complacent about the probability of a rate hike in October. That complacency rests on a few bases. One is that the chairman's top lieutenants speak for him, or at least wouldn't contradict him in public. That was true in the past, but may not be so anymore. In recent weeks, both Fed Vice Chairman Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams gave remarks that indicated they see little urgency in raising interest rates. The markets quickly repriced in favor of a hold in October. Warsh, Jefferson and Williams make up an informal decision-making team atop the Fed known as the troika. Warsh could arguably coordinate with the troika even if he doesn't believe in communicating his own views. But outsiders can't be certain that traditional conventions surrounding the public statements of the New York Fed president and the Fed vice chair have survived the leadership transition. Another assumption is that Warsh broadly accepts the FOMC's view of the economy. "The world has broadly conformed to our expectations," Warsh said in Bangkok of the economy since September. That can be read as saying that relatively hot inflation readings from the consumer and producer price indexes in recent days don't disconfirm the view expressed in the Fed's most recent Summary of Economic Projections released at the conclusion of the September meeting. At the time, the median Fed official believed there would be one more rate hike in 2026 — which left room to pause in October and raise again in December. But Warsh went out of his way at the September press conference to disclaim the SEP. "Those aren't my forecasts," he told a reporter. Warsh set out his own idiosyncratic reading of the economy in detail at a closely watched speech in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, at the end of August. It described the economy as growing strongly, with inflation a greater worry than the jobs market. Warsh's strongly hawkish views then set up the FOMC to unanimously raise interest rates in September. That hawkish position relied heavily on what he sees as loose credit conditions. The Chicago Fed's National Financial Conditions Index has risen about 0.05 points since Jackson Hole but remains negative, indicating financial conditions have tightened but remain loose overall. We can infer these answers, but we won't really know them until the FOMC press conference. Then there is the inflation data. title: Economists: Hot PPI shows Fed's work is not done
summary: 'We see real risks the Fed will deliver another rate hike in two weeks' time,' one Fedwatcher warns
body: Wall Street estimates for the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation indicator now expect an acceleration from the level that prompted the central bank to hike rates last month. The estimates come after a hotter-than-expected producer price index came in at 1.3% Thursday, the biggest monthly gain since March 2022 and more than double the 0.6% consensus. That drove the year-over-year increase to 6.3%, the biggest jump since December 2022. The increase was paced by a 20% rise in gasoline prices. But taking out food, energy and trade services, prices still rose a healthy 0.5%, indicating that inflation was broader than just energy. Seven Wall Street estimates gathered by CNBC show core personal consumption expenditures inflation for September, which will be published later this month, is forecast to rise 0.32%, up from 0.25% in August. Wall Street economists use the consumer price index , released Wednesday, and the PPI to estimate the PCE. "We see real risks the Fed will deliver another rate hike in two weeks' time even as recent Fedspeak tempered expectations for back-to-back increases,'' wrote Kathy Bostjancic, chief economist at Nationwide. Several Fed officials have argued that the Fed does not need to hurry to hike rates, though they have suggested more rate hikes are needed. As a result, Fed futures on Thursday showed just a 29% probability of a hike at the Fed meeting at the end of this month, but a 91% probability of at least one hike by December. A 0.32% increase in PCE would boost the year-over-year core inflation rate to 3.1%, up from 3.01% in August. Estimates ranged from a high of 0.35% from Barclays to a low of 0.29% from Oxford Economics. "The picture is not benign with inflation elevated and intensifying," wrote Alex Pelle, senior U.S. economist at Mizuho Securities. "On the economic data alone, there is little reason for the Fed to hesitate to continue moving the policy rate higher." Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has suggested one litmus test for not hiking is confidence that inflation will return in a timely manner to the Fed's 2% target. Both headline and core PCE inflation have been above target since 2021. They have inched steadily higher since tariffs were introduced in April 2025. The gains have accelerated since the beginning of the Iran war. The Fed prefers the PCE because, compared to the CPI, it believes it more closely resembles how Americans actually spend their money and changes its weightings when consumers change their spending patterns.

title: U.S. Treasury dismisses IMF debt warning and 'messy' forecasting
summary: The exchange comes as U.S. debt exceeds $40 trillion and 10-year Treasury yields remain above 5%, intensifying scrutiny of the fiscal outlook.
body: The International Monetary Fund should check its own forecasting record before criticizing U.S. fiscal policy, David Zervos, newly appointed counselor to the Treasury Secretary , said on Thursday. "When we see pieces on the IMF, it's good to remember how messy their forecasts have been in the past," Zervos said in emailed comments to CNBC. The former Wall Street economist was responding to the IMF's Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, who cautioned during the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Wednesday that strong U.S. economic growth would not be sufficient to put mounting federal debt on a sustainable course. Georgieva was herself responding to U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who told CNBC in August that the U.S. could "grow our way out" of a rising debt-to-GDP ratio, after government debt surpassed $40 trillion . Zervos, formerly chief market strategist at Jefferies, said Thursday: "In 2008, [the IMF's World Economic Outlook] had world growth at 3% and we had the first global contraction in post-world history a year later. We saw them positive on Southeast Asia in 1997 before the collapse." "We saw them very negative on Russia in 2022, and Russia actually barely saw a blip down in growth before it started growing strongly . We saw them very positive on Argentina after their big bailout of $57 billion . And by 2020, Argentina was basically in default again . And the history books go on and on, whether it's Greece, whether it was the transitory call on inflation in the U.S." Many economists warn that mounting U.S. interest payments and a high deficit have raised the risk of an unsustainable debt spiral. However, they are divided on whether the U.S. could be pushed into a true fiscal crisis . The IMF's Georgieva has issued similar warnings to other big economies over the need for fiscal consolidation, telling CNBC on Oct. 7 that her message to France was: "Get your house in order." Other economic institutions are also sounding the alarm over the rising cost of servicing global debt, which topped $365 trillion in the first half of the year . The Institute of International Finance argued in a September report that a "vicious cycle between elections and short-term quick fixes" to debt challenges was reducing the ability to spend money on public services.

title: Analysis: Why a $2 trillion deficit and 5% Treasury yields are becoming America's biggest economic challenge
summary: Treasury yields above 5% are raising borrowing costs for households and the federal government, highlighting the challenge of financing $2 trillion deficits.
body: Long-term bond yields above 5% and a $2 trillion deficit are giving Americans a taste of what a U.S. debt crisis would be like. A true emergency would hurt much more, and isn't baked in. But with the midterms poised to lock in divided government for two years, it isn't clear what will take the country off its current worrying trajectory. Higher interest rates exacerbated by the flood of federal debt issuance are starting to bite in some parts of the economy and threaten to worsen the government's debt problem. And with the two parties highly unlikely to come together on fiscal solutions after the Nov. 3 midterms, any fixes are years off in the future. The housing market is showing signs of slowing as the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage hovers around 7.5%. Pending home sales fell 4% in September, Redfin said Monday, the biggest monthly drop in three years. Mortgage rates track the 10-year Treasury yield . The 10-year has climbed 114 basis points, or hundredths of a percentage point, since the end of February through midday Friday, when the 10-year traded at 5.1%. Several factors are pushing up the 10-year, including the war with Iran, which kicked off on Feb. 28 and precipitated the rise in long-term yields. Oil and diesel prices are up sharply, and that has bond traders asking for more yield to account for the possibility that central banks such as the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates. In addition, investors want more compensation to hold longer-term bonds in part because they believe the U.S. government will continue to flood the market with them. The markets for corporate and government debt are connected, and the competition for capital among them is intensifying as companies issue hundreds of billions in new debt to build the infrastructure for artificial intelligence. Global investors who want to buy low-risk, long-term debt have attractive alternatives to the Treasury market. If the U.S. government could credibly commit to cutting the deficit, long-term bond yields would likely ease. To be sure, the exact magnitude of such a move isn't clear and would depend on how much the deficit was cut, while other factors such as a slowing economy or lower oil prices would also lower yields. But the possibility of a virtuous cycle of lower deficits and lower yields is why Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued that the U.S. ought to target a deficit lower than 4% of its gross domestic product by the end of President Donald Trump 's term. There is almost no way the U.S. will hit that target. The deficit was $1.992 trillion for the 2026 fiscal year, up 12% from last year, data released Friday by the U.S. Treasury showed. That deficit amounts to approximately 6.2% of gross domestic product, based on an estimate of third-quarter GDP. Higher rates make debt reduction tougher. If interest rates stay a half-point above the CBO's expectations, the cumulative deficit over 10 years will come in $1.9 trillion higher, the agency estimates . If rates overshoot by 1.5 points, that adds $6 trillion in deficits. The CBO expects the 10-year Treasury to average 4.3% over that period, compared with 5.1% today. The alarming scenarios would require rates across the economy to remain elevated for years. "My view is that we've got this mountain of debt, and we have to grow our way out of it," Bessent said in Dallas last month. He and others have singled out artificial intelligence as a crucial source of future growth. AI could help but can't fix the problem entirely. It would take a decade of 7.2% growth to balance the budget with growth alone, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget , a research group that advocates for balanced budgets. GDP growth was recently revised up for the second quarter from 1.5% to 2.2% at an annualized rate. The acceleration that quickly would get us to 7.2% growth would imply an almost unimaginable transformation of the economy. Trump will soon enter the final two years of his presidency,

title: UK economy grew 0.1% in August, beating expectations
summary: The U.K. is grappling with a cost-of-living crisis sparked by sticky inflation and surging energy costs.
body: The U.K. economy grew by a better-than-expected 0.1% in the month to August, with production growth offsetting weak output in services and construction. Economists polled by Reuters had been expecting GDP to shrink by 0.1% between July and August. But the reading still marked a slowdown in momentum for British gross domestic product, which grew by 0.4% month-on-month in June and July. Production grew by 0.8%, the U.K.'s Office for National Statistics said in a release on Thursday, while services showed no growth and construction fell by 0.2% in August. On an annual basis, GDP grew by 2.1% in August, beating economists' expectations of 1.7%. The ONS said it marked the highest year-on-year GDP reading since August 2022. The British pound jumped 0.4% against the U.S. dollar following the release, while yields on U.K. government bonds — known as gilts — fell across the curve. The yield on the benchmark 10-year gilt was last seen trading 9 basis points lower at 5.3364%. The U.K., a net energy importer, is currently grappling with a cost-of-living crisis sparked by sticky inflation and surging energy costs in the wake of the Russia-Ukraine war and the Iran war. The government will unveil its closely watched Autumn Budget later this month. It's tasked with sticking to the previous government's so-called fiscal rules aimed at reigning in public debt while delivering on promises to soften the blow of surging consumer costs. Analysts said the slowdown in growth added to pressure facing U.K. finance minister John Healey as he prepares to deliver his first budget on Oct. 28. Joe Nellis, head of economic research at accountancy firm MHA, said in a note that the slowing economy will weigh on Healey's "fiscal headroom" – the amount of leeway the government has to either increase spending or cut taxes. "While continued economic growth should provide some support for tax revenues, the economy remains fragile. Rising debt interest costs have severely constrained fiscal headroom, with long-term government borrowing costs remaining exceptionally high," he said. He added that any decision to raise taxes to balance the books "carries considerable risks," threatening to weaken consumer spending, undermine confidence and discourage corporate investment. But at the same time, Nellis said, significant unfunded spending commitments could unsettle financial markets and push government borrowing costs higher. Scott Gardner, investment strategist at J.P. Morgan Personal Investing, said in a note following the ONS release that while it was positive to see the economy continuing to grow despite global challenges, the outlook for the rest of the year "remains uncertain with a tricky Autumn Budget ahead." "It's unclear right now what fiscal headroom will be left given the servicing of UK debt has increased over the last year. Many will be waiting nervously to see what the Chancellor announces," he said. Sanjay Raja, chief U.K. economist at Deutsche Bank, struck a more optimistic tone. "While we aren't seeing any dramatic course correction (so far), there are signs that the engine of the U.K. economy is slowing from its torrid pace in the first half of the year," he said, noting that consumer-facing services, construction and the IT sectors all slipped from the previous month. But while he said there would "undoubtedly… be some hiccups to come in the run up to year end" as energy prices continue to bite into household incomes and higher interest rates drag on spending and investment, Raja argued that "the U.K.'s resilience story continues." "It's hard to overstate how strong the U.K. performance has been all year," Raja said. "The U.K. economy remains the fastest growing G7 economy. What's more impressive? If you believe the HMRC jobs data, U.K. GDP growth hit 1.8% in the first eight months of the year, with 95k FEWER jobs. Who said productivity growth was dead in the U.K.?"

title: How high inflation became a 'fact of life' in the U.S.
summary: U.S. inflation has stayed elevated for years, raising concern at the Federal Reserve that consumers may come to expect stubbornly high prices.
body: U.S. consumers are in the midst of one of the longest stretches of elevated inflation of the past century. Some are beginning to act like it's a new normal, raising alarm bells for members of the Federal Reserve . Wednesday's consumer price index release showed a 3.7% increase year over year in September. CPI has now registered around 65 months — that's more than five years — of consecutive annual readings above 2%, a widely accepted target for inflation in the U.S. This yearslong spell of high inflation has cast a dark cloud over everyday Americans' view of the economy, and could shape everything from how they budget to how they vote in next month's midterm elections. At the Fed, leaders are left questioning whether consumers' inflationary expectations are becoming too entrenched to rein in. "They're starting to accept high inflation as just a fact of life," Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack wrote in a social media post last week. "That's concerning." The current streak of stubborn inflation ranks among the most persistent in modern U.S. history. The uninterrupted string of above-2% monthly CPI readings is the longest of the 21st century, according to a CNBC analysis of data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The U.S. has seen longer periods on only two other occasions going back to the late 1940s. Since inflation started running above 2% in early 2021, the average CPI reading has sat around 4.5%. The last time a streak had a mean reading that high was during a period ending in the 1980s . Consumers are expecting inflation to accelerate. The one-year inflation outlook in September rose three-tenths of a percentage point to 3.9%, its highest reading in more than three years, according to the New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations released last week. One of the main worries of central bankers is that businesses and consumers may start permanently adjusting their behaviors to account for high prices. That can have ripple effects through the economy. Businesses anticipating rising costs can preemptively hike prices for consumers. Workers expecting sticky inflation will ask for steeper pay raises to get ahead of any sticker shock. All of this can make inflation a self-fulfilling prophecy, rendering the monetary policy tools at the Fed's disposal less effective in slowing price growth. "Inflation expectations have to be anchored for monetary policy to affect the economy in an effective and predictable manner," said Gary Richardson, an economist and former historian at the Fed. "That's got to be number-one goal of any central bank." At this juncture, Fed officials are closely watching to see if and how consumers respond to inflationary pressures. During an event last month, Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari said he heard from a labor union leader that inflation was "worse" than a recession for their members. Kashkari said that conversation influenced how he views the trade-off within the Fed's so-called dual mandate, which calls for stability in prices and maximum employment. At a gathering of economists in Ohio this week, Hammack told the audience that she did not take the fact that long-run inflation expectations have stayed anchored "for granted." With each month that inflation comes in high, she warned that the risk grows of an "inflationary mindset" getting entrenched. Economists widely view interest rate hikes as the Fed's main mechanism for slowing demand and, in turn, putting downward pressure on the annual pace of price growth. title: 'Godzilla El Niño' is wreaking havoc with Philippine central bank's inflation forecasts
summary: The Philippine central bank is running policy scenarios for a severe El Niño on top of the oil shock, with inflation at a three-year high.
body: BANGKOK — The Philippine central bank is planning for a "Godzilla" El Niño on top of a prolonged oil shock, as the Southeast Asian nation tries to rein in inflation from three-year highs. Governor Eli Remolona said Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas now sets policy using scenarios that factor in oil prices and the severity of the weather event. "We have the regular, ordinary El Niño, which is bad, and then we have the Godzilla El Niño, which is really, really bad," he said Wednesday on a panel at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok. The worst of El Niño's impact on prices is still to come, with the effects expected from November through February, he said, adding that maintaining price stability remains the central bank's priority. "We're holding our breath," he said, "but we have to be prepared for the worst." The looming weather risk is adding fresh pressure on one of Southeast Asia's most vulnerable economies. Philippine inflation accelerated to 7.2% in September from 6.1% in August, with rice prices up 18%, according to the Philippine Statistics Authority. The world's biggest rice importer is also exposed to food supply risk. Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel has warned that a fresh drought could squeeze domestic supply . Larger Philippine purchases could add demand to a global market already jolted by El Niño and export curbs. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization has raised its rice price index for six consecutive months to a 20-month high. The central bank lifted its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to 5% in August to keep a lid on the runaway inflation. The BSP should deliver another quarter-percentage hike next week to 5.25%, followed by another same-sized hike in December, according to Aris Dacanay, senior ASEAN economist at HSBC Bank, in a note Wednesday.

title: The latest inflation data is expected to show price increases are accelerating
summary: Economists expect the consumer price index for September to rise 0.6% on the month and 3.6% year over year.
body: Wednesday's closely watched reading on consumer prices could show intensifying inflationary pressures as energy costs keep climbing. Economists polled by Dow Jones expect the headline consumer price index for September to rise 0.6% for the month and to increase 3.6% compared with a year ago. That 12-month number would signal that the rate of price growth is accelerating and moving further from the Federal Reserve 's goal of 2%. So-called core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, is expected to increase 0.2% from August and 2.5% on a 12-month basis. While that would mark a slight slowdown from the prior month, it would be an uptick in year-over-year inflation. Oil-related prices could drive the headline figure even higher, said Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM, a tax firm. Energy costs have been among the biggest drivers of inflation since the U.S. war with Iran began earlier this year. President Donald Trump last week announced loosened diesel restrictions on Russia in a bid to juice the global oil trade, though analysts don't believe it will meaningfully bring down prices. Prices for Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, climbed more than 14% in September, bringing its third-quarter advance to about 42%. Brent prices on Tuesday traded around $105 per barrel. "We've got real upside risk on the September CPI," Brusuelas said. "Typically, when we have these moves in inflation, everyone's models undershoot the actual outcome." Sticky oil prices could also push up costs for items in other, non-energy categories, according to Robert Sockin, chief U.S. economist at asset manager PGIM. In this scenario, it would become harder for the Fed to write off the energy prices surge as a short-term shock that won't necessitate interest rate increases. After announcing its first increase in three years last month, the Federal Reserve signaled in its minutes from that meeting that it will likely have to hike rates again . Fed funds futures traders anticipate the central bank will next lift rates at its December policy meeting, according to CME's FedWatch tool. "The list of reasons to hike rates in our view is long," Sockin said. "Ultimately, we have low confidence in the timing of the Fed's next move, but more conviction on the direction of travel." Wednesday's release is the last reading on CPI before November's midterm elections , which could determine whether the Republican party will keep total control in Washington. Economic confidence across political affiliation has fallen this year, according to the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment data. Compared with Democrats, Republican and independent voters have posted steeper declines in sentiment since the start of 2026, the data shows. Economists forecast that the producer price index, a gauge of inflation facing wholesalers due on Thursday, will rise 0.6% from August to September and 5.5% on a 12-month basis. Both of those numbers would mark a modest acceleration in growth compared with August's release.

body: Gold bulls seem to be perpetually rattling their sabres right now. The war cry is that gold has corrected enough and is now presenting an attractive buying opportunity. Ramped-up, excitable analysts are recommending dollar-cost averaging, while the familiar arguments about money printing, inflation and central bank buying are at the forefront of it all. But The Bradshaw Predictor Model (BPM) is telling me something very different. Gold is still expensive. Momentum remains negative. And a new secular bear market has been confirmed and is now well underway. It is precisely why, despite all the excitement, Iâm staying firmly on the sidelines. Sometimes, the hardest investment decision is resisting the temptation to follow the crowdâ¦ In January 2026, gold reached a 71% overvaluation â its highest since 1983 and a level reached just 6% of the time over the past 56 years. Since then, gold has fallen 31%, retreating from $5,600 to $3,875. Yet hereâs the vexatious part that so many investors appear to be overlooking: despite that correction, gold remains 22% overvalued. For context, goldâs 2008 peak overvaluation was just 25%. What followed? A 34% drawdown. A comparable decline from todayâs price would take gold to $2,550. The correction so far has certainly been significant. But, whisper it, gold is still historically overpriced. A falling price doesnât automatically make an expensive asset cheap. Every new Gold analysis as it publishes, today's technical signal and key levels, live price â on one page. My model estimates that goldâs fair value currently sits at $3,175 . At $3,875, investors are effectively paying $700 more than my model suggests they should. I concede that fair value is an estimate, not a guaranteed destination. Markets can remain irrational for considerably longer than investors might expect. But hereâs my question: when did dollar-cost averaging into an already overvalued asset suddenly become a sensible investment strategy? Buying something simply because its price has fallen is not the same as buying something because it represents good value. Between mid-2013 and early-2025, my model consistently classified gold as undervalued. For more than a decade, investors had an opportunity to accumulate the precious metal at what, in retrospect, were exceptionally attractive prices. Then something changed. Gold moved into overvalued territory in early-2025, eventually reaching a 71% overvaluation earlier this year. Despite the subsequent correction, my model continues to signal that gold is expensive. For me, the opportunity to accumulate has given way to a compelling reason to exercise patience. The question is no longer whether gold deserves a place in an investment portfolio. It is whether todayâs price offers sufficient compensation for the risks involved. Goldâs major peaks in 1974 and 2011 coincided with overvaluations of 70% and 64%, respectively. January 2026 delivered an even higher reading of 71%. Both historical peaks preceded substantial bear-market declines of 46-49%. A comparable decline from Januaryâs $5,600 peak would take gold into the $2,850-$3,000 region. That is the territory where I would start looking for opportunities again. Itâs simple for me. When, in the past, similar valuation extremes have preceded major declines, I would rather pay attention than dismiss the warning signs. History reinforces the message. Goldâs major peaks in 1974, 1980 and 2011 coincided with expensive or bubble valuations. Conversely, its major troughs in 1970, 1976, 2001 and 2022 coincided with cheap or depressed valuations. There is a recurring relationship between valuation extremes and major turning points in the gold market. It isnât a crystal ball, nor does it guarantee a repeat cycle. But it does raise an important question: do we listen to what history is telling us, or simply discard it and charge heedlessly forward? I can already hear the objections. Money printing. body: Silver kicks off the week with a couple of different fundamental influences. Real yields eased into Friday, while the latest verified U.S. manufacturing data shows improvement that remains modest over several months. Together, they offer a bit of a framework for assessing the metalâs monetary and industrial roles, which, of course, we have to pay close attention to. The Treasuryâs 10-year real yield declined from 2.37% to 2.25% . Lower real yields can reduce the opportunity cost of holding precious metals. For silver, the monetary support needs to be considered alongside the outlook for industrial activity as well. The industrial evidence is from October 16 and covers September . The Federal Reserve reported manufacturing output increasing 0.3% after a 0.2% decline in August. Its seasonally adjusted manufacturing index was 98.4 in September, against 98.1 in April, with 2017 equaling 100. September was preliminary, and the preceding months were revised. body: LONDON: Copper prices rose on Monday, supported by a weaker dollar, lower oil prices and a downgrade to Chile’s copper production outlook, though investors remained cautious ahead of Tuesday’s US midterm elections. Benchmark three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange was up 0.7% at $14,251 a metric ton by 1034 GMT. The dollar eased and oil prices fell after talks between Iranian and Qatari officials aimed at pushing for a deal to end the US-Israeli war on Iran. Meanwhile, copper inventories in LME-registered warehouses rose to 293,775 tons, their highest since mid-July, after 20,500 tons were delivered in New Orleans, daily exchange data showed. “The only deliveries we’ve seen onto the LME stocks have been in the US and, arguably, material held there is not having the same impact on the curve -3 as it would if deliveries had been made in Europe or Asia,” said Morgan Stanley analyst Amy Gower. “The market is treating US stocks as largely unavailable for now.” Traders have been shipping copper to Comex-approved warehouses in the US since President Donald Trump ordered a study into potential copper tariffs in February last year. While incentives to move metal to the US have diminished as tariff uncertainty drags on, the risk remains high enough to keep inventories there, with some material also flowing into LME warehouses in the US. On the supply side, Chile’s copper commission, Cochilco, sharply lowered its forecast for the country’s copper production this year and forecast a more modest 2027 recovery than previously expected. Chile is the world’s largest copper producer. body: US Pork Producers Express Gratitude for Long-awaited EPA Data Decision Secretary Rollins Announces 8 Additional Companies Joining USDA’s Product of USA Label Initiative Andrew Wright writes in Southern Ag Today: Earlier this year, an article in Southern Ag Today titled The Outlook for Interest Rates in 2026 examined how interest rates might change in 2026 based on the Federal Open Market Committee’s (FOMC) Summary of Economic Projections . This article reviews those early-2026 projections, compares them with the FOMC’s actual policy decisions, and discusses what changes in the economic environment might mean for interest rates in 2027. Table 1 summarizes the economic projections of the twelve FOMC members at the December 2025 and March 2026 meetings. At the start of the year, most FOMC members believed a federal funds rate between 2.9% and 3.6% was the appropriate path for 2026. At the time, the FOMC’s target range for the federal funds rate was 3.5%- 3.75%, implying a single quarter-point rate cut in 2026 was likely. However, at its September meeting, the FOMC raised the federal funds rate target range by a quarter point to 3.75%-4.0%. In addition, the FOMC’s September Summary of Economic Projections indicated that most members now favored a federal funds rate between 4.0% and 4.4% in 2026 (Table 2). Two factors likely explain the change in the FOMC’s monetary policy path. First, the FOMC’s composition changed this year. In May, Kevin Warsh replaced Jerome Powell as the Chair of both the Federal Reserve and the FOMC. At the same time, four regional Federal Reserve bank presidents rotated off the committee, and four new presidents joined, as is standard practice each year. The addition of five new members may have shifted the board’s composition, leading to a more hawkish stance on inflation. The second factor likely influencing the FOMC’s decisions this year is the trajectory of inflation in 2026, as shown in Figure 2. In January, annual inflation in the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) index, the FOMC’s preferred measure of inflation, was 2.73%. By August, annual inflation had risen to 3.45% due to higher tariffs, the Middle East conflict, and resulting increases in input and energy costs across multiple sectors of the economy (FOMC 2026). These events put pressure on the FOMC to reverse course and raise the federal funds rate. What does this mean for the final two months of 2026 and into 2027? The most likely scenario is higher rates, at least in the short term. If the FOMC’s September projections are accurate, a quarter-point increase at its December meeting would not be unexpected. The long-term outlook is less certain. According to the September summary, the median projection is for the federal funds rate to hold steady at 4.1% next year. How the FOMC manages monetary policy will depend on inflation’s trajectory and the economy’s strength. If the U.S. economy shows signs of a recession, the FOMC may feel compelled to lower rates. If the FOMC raises the federal funds rate in December and keeps the target rate between 4.0% and 4.25% in 2027, expect higher agricultural loan rates as well. Agricultural rates rose in the third quarter of 2026, possibly in anticipation of the committee’s September decision. Figure 2 offers insight into where agricultural rates may end up next year. For most of 2025, the FOMC held the federal funds rate steady between 4.25% and 4.5%. At the same time, long- and intermediate-term agricultural rates were near 8.0%, while short-term rates were closer to 8.5%. The actual rate a borrower receives will depend on their relationship with the lender and their perceived creditworthiness; however, as producers begin planning for 2027, they should expect to pay higher interest rates on operating loans next year. body: Australia’s central bank expected to hit mortgage holders again on Tuesday, as war in Middle East combines with collapsing house prices Australia’s economy is set for a “sharper, longer slowdown”, major bank economists say, as the Reserve Bank is forced to keep interest rates higher to rid the nation of persistent inflationary pressures. The RBA is widely expected to hit mortgage holders with a fifth rate hike on Tuesday, in a move that will push the cash rate to its highest since 2008 amid rising worries the economy could even be tipped into recession. Belinda Allen, the head of Australian economics at CBA, said the extended Middle East conflict, collapsing house prices and a more aggressive central bank would drive real GDP down to just 1% by the middle of next year, nearly half the previous estimate of 1.8%. Growth through 2027 would be barely stronger at an estimated 1.1%, according to the updated projections. Allen said she had expected to see “signs of economic recovery” by the New Year, but now sees the economy “bottoming deeper and later”. This more pessimistic outlook was “mainly given oil has been a lot higher than we had been expecting,” she said. “Most people thought we would see a resolution to the Middle East conflict by now and oil [prices] looking more normal. Alas, that has not been the case.” Instead, Brent crude, the global oil price benchmark, has surged from about $US72 a barrel in early July, to back above $US110 in recent days as the conflict broadens and hopes for a peace deal in the near future have all but disappeared. After Jim Chalmers last month warned the December mid-year budget update would show a more pessimistic economic outlook , analysts at NAB also revealed a major downgrade to their forecasts. Gareth Spence, the bank’s head of Australian economics, said “unemployment might need to rise higher than we thought” in order to get inflation back under control – a view he said reflected recent comments by top RBA officials. The economy would grow below trend over 2027 and 2028, Spence said, echoing the forecast of just 1% growth next year. Spence forecast the key jobless measure would need to rise from 4.7% to as high as 5.4% by the end of next year, as the RBA doubles down on its battle to regain control of inflation. The CBA forecast was more optimistic, seeing unemployment peak at 5.1% over the same timeframe. Either way, the RBA’s multi-year strategy of bringing inflation to heel without sacrificing post-Covid employment gains now looks unlikely to be achieved. As union leaders protested against the anticipated rate hike in front of the RBA’s offices in Sydney on Monday morning, Spence said the risk was that the central bank would have to hike again. The deteriorating economic outlook comes as new data showed Australia’s property slump remained on track to be one of the deepest on record. Shane Oliver, AMP’s chief economist, said home prices could fall by as much as 15% before levelling off late next year, with Sydney property values already down by 10% from their recent peak. Drawing from RBA research, Oliver said a property correction of that magnitude could deliver a substantial hit to the economy, as worried homeowners pull back on spending – a phenomenon known as the “wealth effect”. A weakening property market will also weigh on homebuilding, Oliver said, adding to the multiplying pressures on the economy. While an economic contraction was not his “base case”, he warned there was a “significant and rising” risk of recession, the chance of which would rise to as high as 45% should the RBA hike as expected on Tuesday.

title: US effective federal funds rate holds at 3.88% as Fed maintains interest rate target - Business Upturn
body: The US effective federal funds rate remained unchanged at 3.88% on October 30. The rate was also recorded at 3.88% on October 29. This shows that short term borrowing costs between banks have remained steady following the Federal Reserve 's latest interest rate decision. The latest update comes at an important time for the US economy . The Federal Reserve has been closely watching inflation, employment and economic growth. Its interest rate decisions can affect everything from business borrowing to household spending. For now, the latest figures show no immediate movement in the effective federal funds rate. However, the broader interest rate outlook remains an important issue for investors and financial markets. The effective federal funds rate measures the interest banks charge one another when borrowing money overnight. These transactions help banks manage their daily cash requirements. The latest reading of 3.88% indicates that the rate has not changed from the previous reported level. This is important because even small movements in short term borrowing costs can influence other parts of the financial system. The Federal Reserve does not directly set the effective federal funds rate at a specific daily number. Instead, it establishes a target range. Market transactions between financial institutions then help determine the actual effective rate. The Federal Reserve's official interest rate data also showed the effective federal funds rate at 3.88% across the reported trading days leading up to October 29. This stability suggests that overnight borrowing conditions have remained relatively consistent. It also reflects the current monetary policy environment following the central bank's October meeting. The latest rate reading follows the Federal Open Market Committee's October 28 meeting. The committee decided to maintain its federal funds rate target range between 3.75% and 4%. The decision was approved by a 10 to 2 vote. However, the meeting also revealed a difference of opinion among policymakers. Federal Reserve officials Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack voted against keeping rates unchanged. Both preferred a quarter percentage point increase. This disagreement highlights the difficult position facing the central bank. Some policymakers remain concerned about inflation. Others must also consider how higher borrowing costs could affect economic activity. The Federal Reserve said economic activity was expanding at a strong pace. Domestic spending remained resilient. Productivity growth was also strong, while business investment continued to show strength. However, inflation remained elevated. The central bank indicated that it needed more economic information before determining the appropriate direction of monetary policy. The Federal Reserve continues to work towards its 2% inflation target. This remains one of its biggest priorities. An unchanged effective federal funds rate does not mean that every borrowing cost in the United States will remain the same. However, it provides an important indication of conditions in the short term money market. The federal funds rate influences several other interest rates across the economy. These include rates associated with business loans, credit products and other forms of borrowing. When interest rates remain elevated, companies may become more careful about taking on additional debt. Consumers can also face higher borrowing costs. This can influence spending decisions and business expansion plans. For investors, the latest reading provides another sign that short term interest rate conditions have remained stable following the Federal Reserve's decision. The next important development will be the release of fresh economic data and further comments from Fed officials. title: MU Stock Rallies Premarket After Blowout Q3 Report: JPMorgan Nearly Triples Price Target On AI Demand Boom - Stocktwits
body: JPMorgan nearly tripled its price target on Micron Technology, Inc.’s shares to $1,540 from $550 on Thursday, and reiterated its ‘Overweight’ rating, after the memory chip giant’s record quarterly report. Singling out Micron’s strong outlook and contract wins, JPMorgan said Micron has transformed from being a cyclical commodity producer to a multi-year contracted supplier with downside protection on revenue and margins. More analysts are expected to revise their price targets on MU on Thursday. Micron stock extended its overnight gains to a 17% rise to $1,223.87 in Thursday’s premarket session. Just before the earnings report, Bank of America had bumped its Micron price target to $1,500, while Needham raised it to $1,550. Micron announced 16 contracts with a five-year term, up from just one in the second quarter, and said customers are willingly signing long-term supply agreements amid the prevailing shortage in memory components. The 16 customers have committed $22 billion in orders spanning data center, consumer and automotive markets, with take-or-pay commitments, cash deposits, and pricing floors designed to lock in supply and protect margins. Micron also said that remaining performance obligations - a key indicator of future contracted revenue - for the customer agreements it has entered into so far are around $100 billion. “Our demand for HBM [high bandwidth memory], not just in '27, but even '28 is well above our ability to supply across all the different HBM flavors. And it's also true -- the same thing is also true, by the way, for non-HBM DRAM as well,” Micron Chief Business Officer Sumit Sadana said on the company’s analyst call. Micron said revenue increased 346% to $41.46 billion last quarter, handily beating analysts’ expectations of $35.3 billion. Earnings came in at $25.11 per share, beating expectations of $20.28 per share. The report triggered a sharp rally in shares of peers SanDisk and Western Digital, as well as legacy chipmakers like Intel. Analysts cheered the blowout performance, with particular praise for the durability of the demand.
